equilibrium constant measures how readily that oxide falls apart.
**A large K means decomposition is strongly favoured, so the oxide is unstable.**
**The smallest K belongs to the most stable oxide.**

N₂O  K = 3·5 × 10³³
NO₂  K = **6·7 × 10¹⁶** ✓ smallest by far
NO   K = 2·2 × 10³⁰
N₂O₅ K = 1·2 × 10³⁴ largest
Comparing powers of ten is enough: 10¹⁶ against 10³⁰, 10³³ and 10³⁴. NO₂ is some fourteen
orders of magnitude less inclined to decompose than the next most stable.

is a solid that decomposes on standing at room temperature.

asking what reaction it belongs to. Here the reaction written is the oxide's own destruction,
so the sense is reversed.

Set up the equilibrium table in **moles**, then convert to partial pressures.
PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g)
start:   a      0       0
change: −x     +x      +x
end:   a−x      x       x
**Total moles** = (a − x) + x + x = **a + x**
Write the **degree of dissociation** as α = x/a, so the total becomes a(1 + α) and the mole
fractions are
PCl₅ : (1 − α)/(1 + α)
PCl₃ = Cl₂ : α/(1 + α)
**Partial pressures** are mole fraction × total pressure p, so
Kp = p(PCl₃) · p(Cl₂) / p(PCl₅)
= [pα/(1+α)]² ÷ [p(1−α)/(1+α)]
= p α² / (1 − α²)
**Solve for α.**
Kp(1 − α²) = pα²
Kp = α²(p + Kp)
α² = Kp / (Kp + p)
**α = x/a = (Kp/(Kp + p))^½** ✓
The square root is what distinguishes (c) from (b), and the **(Kp + p)** in the denominator —
not p alone — is what distinguishes it from (a). A quick sanity check: as p becomes very
large, α tends to zero, which is right, since high pressure suppresses a dissociation that
increases the number of molecules.
∴ x/a = (Kp/(Kp + p))^½.

A **Lewis base** is an **electron-pair donor**; a **Lewis acid** is an electron-pair acceptor.
Look at what happens in
I₂ + I⁻ ⟶ I₃⁻
The **iodide ion** has four lone pairs on it. One of those lone pairs is **donated** into a
vacant orbital of the I₂ molecule, forming the new bond that holds the triiodide ion together.
So **I⁻ is the Lewis base** ✓ and I₂, which accepts the pair, is the Lewis acid.
The other options:
(a) I₂ is the **acid**, not the base — it is the acceptor.
(c) I₃⁻ is the **product** of the reaction, the adduct, so it is neither.
This is a good illustration of why the Lewis definition is needed. On the Brønsted–Lowry
picture, an acid donates a proton and a base accepts one — but **there is no hydrogen anywhere
in this reaction**, so Brønsted–Lowry has nothing to say about it. Only the Lewis definition,
which talks about electron pairs rather than protons, can classify it.
The same reaction explains why solid iodine, almost insoluble in pure water, dissolves readily
in potassium iodide solution to give the familiar brown tincture.
∴ I⁻.

A buffer resists a change in pH, and blood must be held between **7·35 and 7·45** — a swing
of even 0·4 units is life-threatening. The system that does most of this work is the
**carbonic acid – bicarbonate** buffer:
**H₂CO₃ / HCO₃⁻** ✓
It is a classic weak acid with its conjugate base, and it works in both directions:
if acid enters the blood, HCO₃⁻ mops it up: HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ ⟶ H₂CO₃
if base enters, H₂CO₃ neutralises it: H₂CO₃ + OH⁻ ⟶ HCO₃⁻ + H₂O

CO₂, and the body controls that by **breathing**. Breathe faster and CO₂ is blown off, pulling
the equilibrium back and raising the pH; breathe slower and CO₂ builds up, lowering it. The
kidneys adjust the HCO₃⁻ side over a longer timescale.
The phosphate pair **H₂PO₄⁻/HPO₄²⁻** (option a) is also a buffer, but it is mainly
**intracellular** and is present in blood at only about a twelfth the concentration, so it is

(b) H₃PO₄/H₂PO₄⁻ buffers near pH 2 and (c) HPO₄²⁻/PO₄³⁻ near pH 12 — both far from blood pH.

The equilibrium is
CO₂ + H₂O + H₂CO₃ ⇌ 2H⁺ + 2HCO₃⁻
with CO₂ on the **left**, among the reactants.
Allowing CO₂ to **escape** removes a reactant. By **Le Chatelier's principle** the system
opposes the loss by shifting **backwards**, towards the left, to replace the CO₂ that has
gone.
Moving backwards **consumes H⁺**, so
[H⁺] **decreases** ⇒ pH = −log[H⁺] **increases** ✓
That disposes of the others: (a) has the pH moving the wrong way, (b) claims no change when
there plainly is one, and (d) says the forward reaction is favoured when in fact the reverse
is.
The everyday demonstration is a bottle of fizzy water. Sealed, it is under CO₂ pressure and
is distinctly acidic, pH about 4. Leave it open and the CO₂ escapes, the equilibrium shifts
left, and the water becomes less sharp as the pH rises towards neutral.
The same chemistry runs in the body, which is why **hyperventilating** — blowing off CO₂ too
fast — raises blood pH and causes respiratory alkalosis, and why breathing into a paper bag,
which puts the CO₂ back, relieves it.
∴ pH will increase.

A **Lewis base donates an electron pair**; a Lewis acid accepts one.
In
I₂ + I⁻ ⟶ I₃⁻
the iodide ion carries four lone pairs. One of them is **donated** into a vacant orbital on
the I₂ molecule, and that donation is the bond which creates the triiodide ion.
So **I⁻ is the Lewis base** ✓, and I₂, the acceptor, is the Lewis acid.
(a) I₂ is the acid, not the base.
(b) I₃⁻ is the **adduct** — the product — so it is neither reactant nor classifiable here.
The reason the Lewis definition is needed at all is visible in the equation: there is **no
hydrogen** anywhere in it. Brønsted–Lowry theory, which defines acids and bases by proton

Read the observations as a Le Chatelier problem.
[Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (pink) + 4Cl⁻ ⇌ [CoCl₄]²⁻ (blue) + 6H₂O
**Observation 1 — at room temperature the mixture is blue.**
**Observation 2 — on cooling it turns pink.**
Cooling therefore drives the equilibrium **backwards**, towards the pink aqua complex.
By Le Chatelier's principle, **cooling favours the exothermic direction**, because the system
opposes the loss of heat by releasing more. So the **reverse** reaction is exothermic, which
means the **forward** reaction is **endothermic**:
**ΔH > 0** ✓
The same conclusion comes from the other direction: warming turns the mixture blue, and
heating favours the endothermic direction, so the forward reaction must absorb heat.
A tidy way to see it is to write heat in as a reactant:
pink + 4Cl⁻ + **heat** ⇌ blue + 6H₂O
Add heat and the system moves right (blue); remove it and the system moves left (pink) —
exactly what is observed.
This colour change is a standard lecture demonstration, and it is reversible as often as you
like by moving the tube between hot and cold water.
∴ ΔH > 0 for the reaction.
